source_refs.note: Topic 23.3.1 (PDF 104-106); the mechanisms, the DNPH equation and Figure 23.2 are redrawn. The Perspex intermediate is named 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile (the caption says '2-ethyl'); '2,4-NDPH' is read as 2,4-DNPH.

blocks.text: Aldehydes and ketones react with hydrogen cyanide to form cyanohydrins (hydroxynitriles). HCN itself is not used directly because it is an extremely poisonous gas; instead it is made in the mixture by slowly adding a mineral acid (HCl) to an aqueous solution of sodium or potassium cyanide and the carbonyl compound.

items: CH3COCH3 + HCN -> (CH3)2C(OH)CN (2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile), KCN/HCl; it is an intermediate in making the polymer Perspex.

blocks.text: Mechanism: HCN is neither a good nucleophile nor a strong enough acid to give many cyanide ions, so a slight excess of KCN is used, leaving some free CN- ions that start the reaction and keep it going at a reasonable rate.

items: CN- attacks the delta+ carbonyl carbon and the C=O pi electrons move onto oxygen, giving an anion: RCHO + CN- <=> RCH(O-)CN.
The anion takes a proton from HCN, giving the hydroxynitrile and regenerating CN-: RCH(O-)CN + HCN <=> RCH(OH)CN + CN-.

blocks.alt: KCN (excess) + HCl gives HCN + KCl, leaving free CN-. A curly arrow from CN- to the delta+ carbon of RCHO and another from the C=O bond to O give the intermediate anion with O-, R, H and CN on the carbon; with H-CN this becomes the hydroxynitrile RCH(OH)CN and CN-.
blocks.caption: The mechanism of nucleophilic addition of HCN (original diagram after the book's scheme).
blocks.long_description: The cyanide ion is the nucleophile and the carbonyl carbon the electrophile. After the attack, the negatively charged oxygen picks up a proton from an HCN molecule, which releases a new cyanide ion, so cyanide acts like a catalyst. Both steps are reversible, but the equilibria lie far to the right, so most carbonyl compounds give high yields of cyanohydrins.

blocks.text: Nitriles can be hydrolysed by dilute acid or aqueous alkali to carboxylic acids or carboxylate ions (topic 23.4.1).

Since aldehydes and ketones are made by oxidising alcohols, alcohols can be made by reducing them. With a reducing agent such as NaBH4 or LiAlH4, aldehydes give primary alcohols and ketones give secondary alcohols: CH3CHO + 2[H] -> CH3CH2OH (NaBH4, water/OH-); CH3COCH3 + 2[H] -> CH3CH(OH)CH3, propan-2-ol (NaBH4, alkaline aqueous solution). The [H] in brackets stands for hydrogen supplied by the NaBH4 to balance the equation; it does not mean atomic hydrogen.

blocks.alt: A hydride ion H- attacks the delta+ carbonyl carbon of RCHO while the C=O electrons move onto O, giving an alkoxide ion; the alkoxide takes H from H-OH, giving the alcohol and OH-. A box adds CH3CHO + 2[H] -> CH3CH2OH (primary) and CH3COCH3 + 2[H] -> CH3CH(OH)CH3 (secondary).
blocks.caption: Reduction of carbonyl compounds by hydride ions (original mechanism after the book's scheme).
blocks.long_description: The reducing agent acts as a source of hydride ions, H-, which are nucleophiles. The hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon, and the oxygen anion formed then takes a proton from water. The C=O group becomes a CH-OH group.

blocks.text: Aldehydes and ketones undergo a condensation reaction with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) to give orange crystalline solids with well-defined melting points. The reagent adds across the C=O group and a molecule of water is then eliminated. For example, ethanal gives orange crystals of ethanal 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone: CH3CHO + H2N-NH-C6H3(NO2)2 -> CH3CH=N-NH-C6H3(NO2)2 + H2O. This reagent is used to identify carbonyl compounds. Carboxylic acids, esters, acyl halides and amides, which also contain a C=O group, do not give this test.

blocks.alt: Ethanal + 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (H2N-NH- on a benzene ring with NO2 groups at positions 2 and 4) gives ethanal 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone (CH3CH=N-NH- on the same ring) + H2O. A test tube shows an orange precipitate; notes say the precipitate's melting point identifies the compound and that acids, esters, acyl chlorides and amides do not react.
blocks.caption: The 2,4-DNPH test for aldehydes and ketones (original diagram after the book's equation and Figure 23.2).
blocks.long_description: The NH2 group of the reagent joins to the carbonyl carbon and water is lost, so C=O becomes C=N. The orange product is easy to purify; its melting point can be compared with tables to identify the original aldehyde or ketone.
